chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Marwak ibn Ubayd, from a man, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
May Allah curse the Qadiriyya, may Allah curse the Kharijites, may Allah curse the Murjiites, may Allah curse the Murjiites. I said, 'You cursed these once, and these twice?'
He said: 'These [the Kharijites] say that those who killed us are believers, so our blood is stained on their clothes until the Day of Judgment.'

Indeed, Allah related about a people in His Book: 'We will not believe in a messenger until he brings us an offering which the Fire consumes.' Say: 'Messengers came to you before me with clear proofs and with that which you demanded; why then did you kill them if you are truthful?'
He said: 'There was a period of five hundred years between the killers and the speakers, but Allah imposed the killing upon them due to their agreement with what they had done.'

key_terms.الْخَوَارِجَ: Kharijites, early Islamic sect known for excommunicating rulers
key_terms.الْقَدَرِيَّةَ: Qadiriyya, a theological sect emphasizing divine decree
key_terms.الْمُرْجِئَةَ: Murjiites, a sect that deferred judgment on sinners

ai.seo_question: Why did the Kharijites curse the killers of the Imams if they considered them believers?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates the theological basis for the repeated cursing of the Kharijites and Murjiites, highlighting their belief that the killers of the Ahl al-Bayt remained believers, thus keeping the Imams' blood ritually 'stained' on their garments. He employs a Quranic analogy of a people demanding a specific sign (an offering consumed by fire) to illustrate how God held them accountable for killing previous messengers who brought that same sign, despite the five-century time gap. This emphasizes the principle of 'al-lazm' (binding consequence), where the killers' internal approval of the murder binds them to the act eternally.
